transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15 | 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Sarah Langley (Oxbridge Head of AI), Rajiv Iyer (Infra), Linda Gomez (Security), Tom Reyes (Compliance)

Summary (auto): initial scoping for on-prem air-gapped deployment. Discussed offline update mechanisms, hardware constraints (no internet egress, vendor firmware), encryption, audit requirements, and pilot sizing.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Ethan is our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Dr. Sarah Langley: Good, thanks. we, you know, are under a time crunch to get a safe, air-gapped inference solution for a clinical decision support feature. privacy regs, yadda yadda.
[00:16] Ethan Patel: great. can you walk us through your current infra? where do you run models today and what are the constraints?
[00:23] Rajiv Iyer: Sure. currently everything sits on-prem in our private DC. no outbound internet from the inference cluster. we have a separate management VLAN that can talk out but production nets are locked down. rack space is limited; we have DGX-style nodes but with older firmware, and our procurement window to buy new GPUs is, uh, six to nine months.
[00:41] Maya Chen: understood. so two constraints: air-gap/no egress and limited hardware refresh cadence. are you looking for Redwood Private (VPC connected) or fully air-gapped on-prem package?
[00:50] Dr. Sarah Langley: fully air-gapped ideally. compliance wants no external egress. but we are open to a hybrid for canary testing if it's recommended.
[00:58] Linda Gomez: and to add, we need HSM-backed key management, immutable audit logs, SOC2-level evidence, and the ability to do offline updates — with chain-of-custody — for model binaries.
[01:08] Ethan Patel: that's all doable in our on-prem product; offline updates are supported via signed artifact bundles that you import. we use a signing key process and provide tooling for air-gapped ingestion. small caveat: the initial onboarding requires a one-time secure window for provisioning the control plane agent, or we can do a fully manual install with signed manifests.
[01:26] Tom Reyes: manual install is preferred. procurement will only allow encrypted USB or physical transfer approved by security. how does Redwood handle artifact signing and verification?
[01:33] Ethan Patel: we use a PKI-based signing flow; artifacts are signed with Redwood's build key and then verified locally against your trust root. we can also support customer-supplied signing keys if you want full control.
[01:42] Rajiv Iyer: If we supply the signing key, does that mean Redwood can't push patches? what is the update cadence then?
[01:48] Maya Chen: Good question. we can do multiple models: 1) Redwood-managed updates — requires a secure provisioning channel; 2) Customer-managed updates — you import bundles and we provide verification tooling; 3) a hybrid where Redwood prepares signed artifacts and an on-site admin performs the import. each has tradeoffs in operational overhead.
[02:06] Dr. Sarah Langley: latency is also critical. real-time inference for triage needs sub-200ms p95. are you able to meet that on our hardware?
[02:14] Ethan Patel: depends on model size and batching. with quantized Llama-family variants or optimized 8-bit models we frequently hit low hundreds ms for single-request scenarios on modern A100s. on older GPUs it will be higher. we should run a micro-benchmark with your actual prompts.
[02:29] Rajiv Iyer: our nodes are two-year old A100s but with older drivers; also, we run on-prem virtualization that adds some overhead. we need a benchmark that mirrors our stack.
[02:38] Ethan Patel: absolutely. for the pilot we recommend a small benchmark harness that runs inside your network — we'll supply a lightweight runner that you can execute in air-gap mode and share logs.
[02:47] Linda Gomez: on encryption: data at rest and in transit must be FIPS-compliant, and keys must be stored in our HSM. Redwood supports KMS integrations?
[02:56] Maya Chen: yes, we support customer KMS/HSM integrations. for private on-prem installs we integrate with common HSM vendors via PKCS#11; we can document required interfaces.
[03:05] Tom Reyes: audit logs are a big ask. we need tamper-evident logs and exportable records for audits. retention policy of at least seven years for certain artifacts.
[03:14] Ethan Patel: we ship an audit collector that writes signed events to append-only storage — for air-gapped, that can be local disk with export tooling. we'll also provide schema for logs so you can pull them into your SIEM.
[03:23] Dr. Sarah Langley: Great. On models: we prefer open weights but are open to Redwood-hosted variants. how do you handle pinning versions and rollbacks?
[03:31] Maya Chen: you can pin model versions in the config. rollbacks are supported; we keep signed artifacts for previous versions so you can revert without egress.
[03:38] Rajiv Iyer: performance tuning — is continuous KV cache supported in air-gapped mode?
[03:44] Ethan Patel: yes, KV cache is local to the runtime. continuous batching and cache warming works the same; only telemetry scrubbed for PII goes out if you enable telemetry — which you'd disable in air-gapped.
[03:55] Linda Gomez: can we get a list of telemetry fields Redwood collects by default? we need to ensure no PHI leaves the environment.
[04:01] Maya Chen: absolutely, we'll send a telemetry matrix. in air-gapped deployments telemetry is off by default, and any optional export must be explicitly configured with PII redaction.
[04:10] Dr. Sarah Langley: okay, what's the proposed pilot? timeline?
[04:14] Maya Chen: recommended pilot scope: 1) hardware survey and compatibility check; 2) install the runtime in an isolated test rack with a representative model (we suggest a quantized open model); 3) run benchmark harness for latency/cost; 4) a week of controlled traffic to validate stability. typical pilot is 3-6 weeks end-to-end.
[04:31] Tom Reyes: budget and procurement are constraints. if we need new GPUs, that will push timelines. what are resource recommendations for 200 qps with 100 token responses?
[04:40] Ethan Patel: 200 qps at 100 tokens is substantial for synchronous low-latency workloads — you'd likely need a pool of dedicated GPUs with batching; rough estimate: 4-6 A100s depending on quantization. but we'll size after we see your exact prompt mix.
[04:53] Rajiv Iyer: our noise here is bursty; do you support autoscaling within the data center?
[04:58] Ethan Patel: autoscaling in air-gapped is manual or via your internal orchestrator; Redwood Dedicated autoscaling features assume some control-plane connectivity. for fully isolated, we provide guidance and scripts to automate node scaling via your orchestrator.
[05:10] Dr. Sarah Langley: security question: does Redwood have SOC2 and ISO certifications?
[05:15] Maya Chen: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified; we'll share the report under NDA. for private on-prem we also provide an architecture security whitepaper.
[05:24] Linda Gomez: and for legal — we need to confirm data residency and contract clauses about model outputs and IP.
[05:30] Maya Chen: understood, legal can follow up; we'll include standard clauses and can negotiate enterprise terms for on-prem.
[05:36] Rajiv Iyer: firmware: our vendor requires signed firmware for GPUs and disallows certain kernel modules. any special dependencies from Redwood runtime?
[05:44] Ethan Patel: our runtime tries to be lightweight; we do require some kernel modules for GPU drivers and shared memory but can provide a list. some customers run in containers with --privileged flags; others use our appliance installer. we'll coordinate with your vendor constraints.
[05:58] Dr. Sarah Langley: okay, any talk about fallback? if a model fails how do we degrade gracefully?
[06:03] Maya Chen: you can configure fallback policies to a smaller model or a cached response. in air-gapped mode you should provision a small, highly-available model locally for critical paths.
[06:12] Tom Reyes: we also need explainability and audit trails for decisions made by models for compliance. do you support request/response hashing and lineage?
[06:20] Ethan Patel: yes, we support request/response hashes and saved prompt snapshots (redacted) to provide lineage. all stored locally in air-gapped deployments unless you export them.
[06:28] Dr. Sarah Langley: can we get an example deployment topo?
[06:31] Maya Chen: we'll share a reference architecture diagram — that will include control-plane agent options, the runtime nodes behind a load balancer, HSM connectivity, and log collectors.
[06:40] Rajiv Iyer: about cost: on-prem licensing model? is it per GPU, per node, or subscription?
[06:46] Maya Chen: for private on-prem we typically do a subscription plus a node-license tier or reserved capacity approach. we'll propose a pricing model tailored to your pilot sizing.
[06:54] Linda Gomez: we need the SLA details — uptime, latency guarantees, and support response times.
[06:59] Maya Chen: SLA varies by enterprise tier; for Dedicated/Private we offer SLAs and 24/7 support options. we'll include SLA language in the proposal.
[07:06] Dr. Sarah Langley: Great. any integration concerns with our existing feature store/vector DB?
[07:11] Ethan Patel: we can integrate with your vector DB over local network; if your DB is air-gapped we'll need connector details. we also support local embedding generation so you can store vectors internally.
[07:21] Rajiv Iyer: one more thing — are there any licensing restrictions on models? like does Redwood ship certain open models with additional redistributions terms?
[07:29] Maya Chen: model licensing is per-model. we curate a catalog of open models; we surface license info. for some models we provide redistributable artifacts, for others you may need separate agreements.
[07:40] Dr. Sarah Langley: ok good. let's talk pilot success criteria.
[07:44] Maya Chen: success criteria: 1) p95 latency under threshold (you define; you said sub-200ms), 2) deterministic rollout process for offline updates with signed artifacts, 3) auditability and KMS integration validated, 4) stability under representative traffic for one week.
[07:58] Tom Reyes: acceptable. please include sign-off gates for compliance review.
[08:03] Maya Chen: will do.
[08:06] Ethan Patel: quick question on networking: do you allow a jump host for provisioning, or is that prohibited?
[08:12] Rajiv Iyer: jump host allowed under very restrictive conditions; must be in our management VLAN and pre-authorized.
[08:17] Ethan Patel: that's workable — provisioning can use a controlled jump host or be fully offline.
[08:21] Dr. Sarah Langley: anything else from Redwood?
[08:24] Maya Chen: we'll send the SOC2, telemetry matrix, on-prem install checklist, and a proposed pilot SOW. Ethan will set up a hardware survey call.
[08:33] Linda Gomez: we'll review and get procurement involved. expect some internal redaction requests.
[08:38] Maya Chen: sounds good.
[08:40] -- Transcript continues with Q&A and small clarifications --
[10:12] Ethan Patel: (note) regarding offline updates, you can elect to hold keys in your HSM and only allow signed manifests that reference a hash. this gives you chain-of-custody.
[12:20] Dr. Sarah Langley: any performance regressions when using quantized weights vs full FP16?
[12:26] Ethan Patel: negligible for many workloads; sometimes quality tolerance requires FP16 — we'll evaluate on your prompt set.
[15:05] Rajiv Iyer: we'll need a small proof-of-concept before committing to a procurement cycle.
[15:12] Maya Chen: understood, pilot-first approach is standard.
[18:00] Tom Reyes: legal will want indemnities and clarity on output ownership.
[18:05] Maya Chen: noted; legal will follow up with standard terms.
[25:00] Dr. Sarah Langley: last practical thing — how often do you need to rotate certificates/keys in air-gapped?
[25:06] Ethan Patel: rotation is configurable; typically customers rotate signing keys every 12 months, but we can support shorter cycles.
[30:00] Maya Chen: ok recap: we'll send artifacts (SOC2, telemetry, install checklist, SOW draft), Ethan will schedule hardware survey, customer to provide sample prompts and traffic profile. any objections?
[30:14] Dr. Sarah Langley: none.
[30:17] Rajiv Iyer: fine.
[30:18] Linda Gomez: fine.
[30:19] Tom Reyes: cool.
[30:21] Maya Chen: great — thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

End of transcript.
